SURGO × UNIVERSITY OF MANITOBA · CÔTE D’IVOIRE

Demand, services and modern contraceptive use

Updated FP-provider-only Rural/Urban supply assignment. Rural women receive the valid-response means of rural FP facilities in their département; urban women receive the corresponding urban means. An exact cell with zero eligible FP facilities would receive a flagged whole-département average; no fallback is needed in this source. Planning heatmaps and categories continue to use pooled département averages. Eligibility uses s2_5_sp = 1 for FP services generally; it does not additionally require on-site provision (s5_1). Daily provision replaces counseling, cleaned stockout burden replaces popular-product stock, and health beliefs use PB2A only. Main classifications use zero-centered average z-scores. Demand indicators remain personal in models; Rural/Urban residence remains a covariate.

Joint evidence helps identify where reported concerns coincide with service weaknesses. Associations and relative planning categories do not establish causal binding constraints or budget allocations.

Supply profiles remain incomplete in five surveyed areas. Bonon, Facobly, Gohitafla and Taabo have no linked facility records. Daoukro has general FP providers but undefined free-product and daily-provision proportions. They remain supply-unassessed; missing values are not zeros. The stock appendix documents the retained UoM stockout definition.
Main score and classification
  1. Calculate six concern prevalences using valid-domain answers and WEIGHT; restrict facilities to raw s2_5_sp = 1 and average valid facility values separately by measure, without facility weights. Valid zeros/FALSE remain included.
  2. Align supply direction first: stock continuity = 1 − stockout burden; other five inputs remain favorable. Standardize each component against the mean and sample SD of its side’s complete-département reference set. Départements contribute equally.
  3. Average six standardized components separately on each side. A missing component prevents a complete score. Higher demand means more concern; higher favorable supply means stronger provision.
  4. Flag demand strictly above 0.000000; favorable supply strictly below 0.000000. Both cutoffs equal zero, the final-score mean. Ties are unflagged; model supply risk is negative readiness. Scores are averages of six standardized components, not percentage-point differences.

Demand references use 82 départements with all six demand percentages; supply references use the same 77 complete départements for every supply component. Thus each final score has mean zero over its own stated reference set. These are equal-département references, not the overall weighted-woman or pooled-facility heatmap row. The four unmatched areas and Daoukro’s undefined free-product and daily-provision measures remain supply-unassessed. Categories are relative planning signals.

Classification summary. 18 areas have both sides flagged, 20 demand only, 19 supply only, 20 neither and 5 supply-unassessed. Component estimates and response coverage provide context for interpreting the classifications.

Both-flagged départements are included on each flagged side, so groups overlap. Demand totals also include known concern flags in supply-unassessed areas; those areas are not classified as demand-only. A département contributes to three components, so percentages do not sum to 100%. These are relative component patterns, not service-standard failures. Stockout burden is higher = worse; other raw supply measures are higher = better. These rules are reversed as needed before standardized component ordering.

Short- and long-acting options together means at least one long-acting and three short-acting categories at the same facility. Free provision and training average within-facility proportions; they are not shares of facilities offering any free product or having any trained provider. The confidence indicator is unchanged: it measures confidence choosing a method or managing side effects, not objective knowledge.

04 · ADJUSTED ASSOCIATIONS

Modern use in relation to personal concerns and local services

All models: 3,951 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 2,262 modern users across 77 départements. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Côte d’Ivoire-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, département-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

Score assigned to each womanConstructionObserved model variation
Demand risk scoreStandardize her own six demand responses using weighted item means and population SDs among valid FPN2 = 1 women; average all six. Her département or residence does not determine this score.62 distinct values across 3,951 women.
Supply risk scoreConvert stockout burden to continuity = 1 − burden; standardize her six favorable département–Rural/Urban measures against the fixed means/SDs of the same 77 complete départements used for planning. Average and reverse the sign: higher = weaker provision.124 distinct numeric scores across 124 modeled département–residence profiles in 77 départements. No fallback is required in this source.
ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.35 (0.26–0.48) and the supply score odds ratio 0.85 (0.69–1.05) per one original average-z index point. These are adjusted associations on the same women. Read the intervals against 1 and consult the joint tests below; overlap with 1 means the direction is not resolved at that confidence level. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.15 (0.08–0.29); health beliefs have OR 0.67 (0.52–0.85); low method confidence has OR 0.66 (0.52–0.85). These individual intervals are pointwise. The six-indicator joint test has Holm p 0.230 with 1.06 effective denominator degrees of freedom, so its joint evidence must be assessed alongside the effective degrees of freedom. The heatmap displays these concerns alongside recorded service conditions; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

Interpretation of results. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -40.1 percentage points for opposition and -8.3 points for health beliefs. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps summarize adjusted differences in predicted modern contraceptive use; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

Interpret this item cautiously. Healthcare permission barriers have OR 1.30 (1.07–1.57) and an adjusted difference of +5.2 points. This does not mean restrictions improve use: the item concerns general healthcare permission, and confounding, selection and reverse direction remain possible.

DEFINITIONS AND VERIFICATION

Measures, denominators and interpretation

Demand domains and unknown responses
DomainQuestion and coding
Healthcare permission barriersHS7C: 1 = permission to see a doctor is a challenge; 2 = no. General healthcare permission, not FP-specific partner approval.
Anticipated social stigmaPB7B/C: 1/2 on either item about being seen or what others would say. Zero requires both valid 3/4 responses.
Health / side-effect beliefsPB2A only: 1/2 indicates perceived health problems; 3/4 indicates no concern; other responses remain unresolved. PB2B/C are not components. This is a belief, not personally experienced side effects.
Future-fertility concernsMP4_a–f reversible-method concerns, requiring coherent MP4_a–i 0/1 selections, no none-plus-method contradiction, an explicit selection or none, and MP4_99 = 0. Sterilization items MP4_g/h do not create a concern.
Low method knowledge · retained labelMC5A/B: low confidence choosing a suitable method or handling side effects/switching (3/4 on either). This is confidence/self-efficacy, not objective knowledge. Zero requires both valid 1/2 answers.
Opposes family planningFP1: against (3/4) versus in favor (1/2). Unfamiliarity (5), no opinion (99) and other special responses remain unresolved.

A known positive establishes an any-concern flag; zero requires valid negatives on every included item. Remaining combinations stay unresolved. These questions are not restricted to married women or nonusers. The retained knowledge label measures subjective confidence.

Supply definitions and response coverage
MeasureCalculation and interpretation
Short + long-acting offeringMean of UoM one_larc_3_sa_offer, joined as share_offer_larc_and_3_sa: share meeting the original ≥1 long-acting plus ≥3 short-acting product/category rule.
Free-product provisionMean of valid facility p_free_prod, joined as mean_p_free_prod. A value of 60% means the average reporting facility provides 60% of its recorded products free; not that 60% of facilities offer any free method.
Trained-provider shareMean of valid facility p_train proportions, using original UoM personnel/topic eligibility. Not the percentage of facilities with at least one trained provider.
Daily provision of offered modern methodsUse s5_2a, b2m/b3m, c, d, e, f, g3a/g5a. Count seven categories: pills, injectables, male/female condoms, emergency contraception, IUD and implants. Combine injectable/implant variants using the most frequent recorded offered variant, counting each method class once. Within each FP facility, Daily categories (code 1) / categories recorded as Daily, Weekly, Bi-monthly or Monthly (codes 1–4). Not at all (5) is excluded from the offered denominator; -9/unknown is not zero. A zero denominator is undefined. Average valid facility ratios equally. This is reported frequency, not proof of daily access or clinical adequacy.
At least one LARC in stockMean of one_larc_stockin, joined as share_stocked_1plus_larc. The country-wide three-LARC indicator is constant FALSE and cannot be standardized; this existing joined alternative is explicitly used.
Stockout burdenAverage original cleaned p_any_stockout among confirmed FP providers. It is the average facility product-group share classified as having current or recent stockouts under UoM coding, not the percentage of facilities with a stockout. Retain the supplied definition. Higher raw burden = worse; use 1 − burden as continuity before scoring/PCA. Numerical completeness does not establish complete raw responses.

Valid zero/FALSE values are included; unknown and undefined values are excluded from each measure’s denominator. Within-facility proportions are averaged equally, rather than replaced by pooled product/personnel ratios. All averages restrict to raw s2_5_sp = 1 (general FP provision, not an on-site requirement): 2,370 confirmed FP providers in 78 surveyed départements. Daily provision has 2,249 defined facility ratios and 121 undefined. Original cleaned stockout burden has 2,370 numeric values. Counseling and popular-product stock are not selected components.

Daoukro has 19 general FP-service providers among 21 source records; all 19 report No to on-site provision (s5_1). Their product questions are largely Not applicable, and both free-product and daily-provision proportions are undefined. Their recorded free/nonfree product counts yield undefined p_free_prod; no zero filling or unapproved repair is applied. The other measures can still be displayed. Daily ratios are conditional on recorded offered categories, including partial method responses; higher daily provision does not by itself establish broad choice or adequate access.

Survey design, adjustment and model sample

All models use original WEIGHT and département-clustered CR2 covariance with Satterthwaite intervals. Recorded IDZD census districts support overview intervals and an inference sensitivity; original strata/FPC are unavailable. Adjust for age, age², education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. No random effects or interactions are fitted.

The model comparison uses 3,951 women, including 2,262 modern users. The overview retains all 4,292 women in need. Assigned residence supply is complete for 4,200; 92 lack a complete profile (49 unmatched and 43 in Daoukro). Models additionally require known demand, outcome and covariates. All five primary models and the five PCA models share the same eligible women. Health uses PB2A only; the remaining demand definitions are retained. Women lacking a complete supply profile remain in the overview but are excluded from these common models.

APPENDIX B · STOCK MEASURE AND SOURCE QUALIFICATIONS

How stockout burden contributes to the supply score

The selected measure is the mean of cleaned p_any_stockout among FP providers: 2,370 numeric records in the linked départements. A value of 30% means the average facility has 30% of its assessed product groups classified as having current or recent stockouts under the UoM definition. It is not the percentage of facilities with any stockout, and 70% continuity is not simply 70% current availability.

Before scoring, continuity = 1 − burden. Standardize continuity alongside the five other favorable measures; average all six for readiness. The negative is supply risk. Greater burden therefore lowers readiness and raises risk.

Original cleaned values and product-group definitions are retained and verified against the supplied UoM export. Numeric completeness does not prove complete raw responses. The existing CDI extraction uses lettered stock items and does not include the unlettered male-condom current-stock question; unknown-response rules also affect derived classifications. The indicator describes assessed groups in the supplied code, rather than a newly verified all-method stock measure. No upstream repair is silently introduced.

APPENDIX C · PCA AND MODEL ROBUSTNESS

Alternative scores from the same personal and residence-specific inputs

Separate weighted PCAs use six personal demand and six assigned département–residence supply components, including daily provision and favorable stock continuity. Demand PCA uses 4,054 women; supply uses 4,200 women across 124 complete département–residence profiles, weighted by represented women’s summed WEIGHT.

Interpretation. Demand PC1 captures 27.0% of input variation; supply PC1 38.0%. Supply PC1 has mixed signs: Trained-provider share load negatively. Its negative is a pattern score, not uniformly worse provision. Supply PC1 does not exceed the exploratory 95th-percentile permutation reference; it remains a prespecified sensitivity score, not a validated one-dimensional supply scale. Coefficients describe input variation, not causal effects or investment decisions.

The same five modern-use models using PCA scores

All models: 3,951 women with original SURGO FPN2 = 1, including 2,262 modern users across 77 départements. Outcome: current modern use = 1; confirmed traditional-only use or nonuse = 0. Adjust for age + age², Côte d’Ivoire-specific education, partnership, fertility goal and Rural/Urban residence. Use WEIGHT, département-clustered CR2/Satterthwaite intervals, and no random effects or interactions.

ModelPredictors alongside the same covariates
1 · Demand scorePersonal demand score
2 · Supply scoreAssigned supply risk score
3 · Both scoresPersonal demand score + assigned supply risk score
4 · Six demand indicatorsEach woman’s six demand indicators separately
5 · Six indicators + supplySix personal demand indicators + assigned supply risk score

Key finding. In Model 3, the demand odds ratio is 0.62 (0.56–0.69) and the supply score odds ratio 0.94 (0.88–1.01) per one oriented PC1 unit. These are adjusted associations on the same women. Read the intervals against 1 and consult the joint tests below; overlap with 1 means the direction is not resolved at that confidence level. These do not allocate a percentage of nonuse to either side.

Planning interpretation. The curves show how predicted modern use varies with each score for the same women, holding other predictors at their observed values. Their levels and uncertainty are easier to interpret than odds ratios. They are adjusted cross-sectional comparisons, not expected gains from removing barriers. An uncertain supply slope does not establish adequate services.

Which reported concerns accompany lower use?

Models 4 and 5 retain personal responses separately. Model 5 also includes the same contextual supply score. The supply-only model is Model 2, shown again for reference.

Key finding. In Model 5, opposition to family planning has OR 0.15 (0.08–0.29); health beliefs have OR 0.67 (0.53–0.85); low method confidence has OR 0.66 (0.51–0.85). These individual intervals are pointwise. The six-indicator joint test has Holm p 0.238 with 1.04 effective denominator degrees of freedom, so its joint evidence must be assessed alongside the effective degrees of freedom. The heatmap displays these concerns alongside recorded service conditions; these associations do not establish which intervention would be most effective.

Interpretation of results. The adjusted present-versus-absent difference is -40.0 percentage points for opposition and -8.3 points for health beliefs. The model predicts the same women under each response setting, retains their supply and other characteristics, and averages using WEIGHT. These gaps summarize adjusted differences in predicted modern contraceptive use; they are not intervention-effect estimates.

PCA interpretation. Supply PC1 has mixed signed coefficients despite favorable input alignment; inspect the updated loadings below. Its negative is labeled a supply pattern score. It is not a monotonic supply-risk index, and its association cannot be interpreted as the effect of worsening every service domain.

Each joint model has two tests. Demand tests its one score coefficient or all six concern coefficients together; supply tests its one score coefficient. Geographic leverage and uncertainty

Unequal département contributions mean nominal geographic count does not guarantee precise inference. Effective denominator degrees of freedom are reported for every joint test. Very low degrees of freedom make a block test weak; lack of joint evidence does not establish no demand role or invalidate every pointwise association.
